summary: A Space.com reference article explaining Earth's average surface temperature, how global temperature is measured, and the planet's temperature extremes. It also covers how temperatures are changing, citing NOAA and NASA data showing a long-term warming trend and the influence of human-driven climate change. The article concludes with resources and a bibliography.
one_line: Space.com explainer on Earth's average surface temperature, how global temperature is measured, record extremes, and ongoing warming.
key_facts: The average surface temperature on Earth is approximately 59 degrees Fahrenheit (15 degrees Celsius), according to NASA.
The 10 warmest years in recorded human history have all occurred since 2010.
NASA announced that 2023 was Earth's hottest summer on record (since at least 1880).
Based on NOAA's temperature data, 2020 was the second warmest year ever recorded, just behind 2016.
The coldest temperature measured on Earth was at Vostok Station in Antarctica, reaching minus 128.6 degrees F (minus 89.2 degrees C) on July 21, 1983.
El Azizia, Libya, held the top hot spot for 90 years until the World Meteorological Organization invalidated its 136.4 degrees F (58 degrees C) reading from Sept. 13, 1922 in 2012.
The hottest air temperature currently recognized was 134 F (56.7 C) at Greenland Ranch (Furnace Creek) in Death Valley, Calif., on July 10, 1913.
A higher surface temperature of 159.3 F (70.7 C) was recorded by a Landsat satellite in 2005 in the Lut Desert in Iran.
NOAA reported average surface temperatures on Earth rose 1.71 degrees Fahrenheit (0.95 degrees Celsius) between 1880 and 2016.
In 2015, 159 nations ratified the Paris Agreement, aiming to halt warming at 2.7 degrees F (1.5 degrees C) above pre-Industrial Age average temperature.
NASA's GISS measures global surface temperature change relative to the 1951 to 1980 average, and found 2020 global average temperatures were 1.84 degrees F (1.02 degrees C) above that mean.
NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies assumes temperature anomalies are about the same up to about 1,200 kilometers from a station.
Temperatures on Venus reach more than 880 degrees Fahrenheit (471 degrees Celsius), while Mars' average temperature is minus 80 degrees F (minus 60 degrees C).
During the last ice age, when northeastern North America was covered by more than 3,000 feet of ice, the global average temperature was only 5 to 9 degrees cooler than today, according to NASA.
At any given time, the hottest and coldest places on Earth are probably almost 100 degrees F (55 degrees C) apart, according to NOAA.

entities.role: Source of the 59 F (15 C) average surface temperature figure and the 2023 hottest summer announcement; also cited for the ice age temperature comparison

entities.name: NOAA
entities.role: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration; provided temperature data showing 2020 was the second warmest year and reported the 1880-2016 warming trend

entities.name: World Meteorological Organization
entities.role: Keeps the official extreme temperature records and stripped El Azizia, Libya of its record in 2012

entities.name: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS)
entities.role: Measures global surface temperature change relative to the 1951 to 1980 average

entities.name: Vostok Station
entities.role: Location in Antarctica where the coldest temperature measured on Earth was recorded in 1983

entities.name: Oymyakon, Russia
entities.role: Small village in Siberia described as the coldest inhabited place

entities.name: El Azizia, Libya
entities.role: Former holder of the hot spot record for 90 years, invalidated by the WMO in 2012

entities.name: Death Valley
entities.role: Location of Greenland Ranch (Furnace Creek), where the highest recognized air temperature was recorded

entities.name: Lut Desert
entities.role: Location in Iran where a Landsat satellite recorded a surface temperature of 159.3 F in 2005

entities.name: Paris Agreement
